interest: This file provides valuable historical insight into how the U.S. State Department and West Coast business leaders monitored Japan's racial policies, internal minority relations, and evolving alignment with Nazi Germany between 1933 and 1941. It highlights the intersection between domestic American immigration administration on the Pacific Coast and foreign affairs in East Asia, showing how commercial figures like Wallace M. Alexander intervened to advocate for culturally sensitive immigration officials. Most significantly, the correspondence and consular reports document the nuanced and pragmatic nature of Japanese policy toward Jewish refugees: while Tokyo publicly disavowed Nazi-style racial persecution and maintained non-discriminatory rhetoric, it quietly cooperated with Berlin to limit transit visas and avoid domestic congestion. The documents also illustrate early manifestations of anti-Semitism in Japan tied to economic grievances (the General Electric patent dispute) as well as early Japanese interest in African Americans.
overview: This State Department file (894.4016), covering the period from April 19, 1933 to May 22, 1941 (with a 1953 archival charge-out slip), documents U.S. diplomatic tracking of race problems, minority relations, and anti-Semitism in Japan. Early cross-reference sheets note Nazi influence inspiring an anti-Semitic rally organized by opponents of General Electric patents in Tokyo in 1933, as well as a proposed 1935 tour of Japan by African Americans promoted by S. S. Firestone. The bulk of the file comprises a December 1938 correspondence between San Francisco businessman Wallace M. Alexander and State Department Political Adviser Stanley K. Hornbeck concerning the appointment of a sympathetic Commissioner of Immigration and Naturalization in San Francisco and inquiries into reports that Jewish professors in Tokyo universities were dismissed under Nazi German pressure. Internal State Department memoranda and Hornbeck's response clarify that while Japan publicly disclaimed discrimination under the German-Japanese cultural pact, informal understandings between Tokyo and Berlin likely restricted passports and entry for German Jewish refugees. The file concludes with a May 1941 consular report cross-reference from Kobe detailing Japanese instructions to European consulates to halt transit visas for Jewish refugees until domestic congestion cleared, while noting that Japanese public opinion and press coverage remained unhostile.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 363 regarding an anti-Semitic mass meeting held in Japan by opponents of General Electric patents.
keywords: Society Opposing the General Electric Patents
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference sheet (Document File Note) referencing Despatch No. 363 of April 19, 1933, from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo, originally filed under 894.543 General Electric Co./1. The despatch reports on a mass meeting held by the 'Society Opposing the General Electric Patents,' at which a majority of speakers made the Jewish race the object of attack. Grew notes that Nazi anti-Semitic activities in Germany undoubtedly exerted some influence in Japan.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 363 from Tokyo on Anti-Semitic Meeting

subfiles.about: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 1458 concerning an announced tour of Japan by African Americans promoted by S. S. Firestone.
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference sheet referencing Despatch No. 1458 of September 1, 1935, from Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville in Japan, originally filed under 032 American Negroes (Japan)/1. The despatch concerns an announced tour of Japan by American Negroes promoted by S. S. Firestone.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 1458 from Tokyo on African American Tour of Japan

subfiles.about: Letter recommending qualifications for the San Francisco immigration commissioner post and inquiring into rumors of anti-Semitic dismissals of Jewish professors in Tokyo universities.
subfiles.summary: Wallace M. Alexander of Alexander & Baldwin, Ltd. writes to State Department Political Adviser Stanley K. Hornbeck, offering congratulations on Hornbeck's marriage. Alexander urges that the new Commissioner of Immigration and Naturalization in San Francisco be familiar with and sympathetic toward Oriental peoples, praising the cooperative tenure of the late Commissioner E. C. Cahill. Alexander also inquires into press reports alleging that Jewish professors in Tokyo universities had been dismissed due to pressure from Germany, noting that Japanese contacts in California denied that any such measures were taken or contemplated. The letter concludes on page 5 with holiday wishes and the signature of William H. Kennedy.
subfiles.title: Letter from Wallace M. Alexander to Stanley K. Hornbeck on Immigration Post and Jewish Professors in Japan

subfiles.about: Internal memorandum recommending Department responses to Wallace M. Alexander regarding the San Francisco immigration vacancy and Japanese policy toward Jews.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs advises Stanley K. Hornbeck on replying to Wallace M. Alexander's letter of December 20, 1938. The memorandum advises that Hornbeck cannot appropriately intervene in an appointment falling under the Secretary of Labor, though Alexander could write to the Labor Department directly. On the Jewish question, the memo drafts text noting that Tokyo's Foreign Office spokesman declared on November 25 that the German-Japanese cultural pact entailed no discrimination against Jewish residents or anti-Nazi German teachers, but adds confidentially that Berlin and Tokyo likely share an understanding restricting passports for German Jews seeking entry into Japan.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Division of Far Eastern Affairs to Stanley K. Hornbeck Regarding Alexander Letter

subfiles.about: Memorandum forwarding an extract from Wallace M. Alexander's letter concerning the San Francisco immigration commissioner post for potential interest to the Department of Labor.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations, addresses a memorandum to Under Secretary of State Sumner Welles regarding a letter received from Wallace M. Alexander of Alexander & Baldwin, Ltd. Hornbeck describes Alexander as a prominent and public-spirited West Coast businessman. He quotes Alexander's recommendation that the next Commissioner of Immigration and Naturalization in San Francisco be sympathetic to and familiar with Oriental peoples, suggesting the paragraph might interest the Department of Labor.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Sumner Welles Regarding San Francisco Immigration Post

subfiles.about: State Department reply to Alexander addressing the San Francisco immigration commissioner vacancy and Japanese policy toward Jewish residents and refugees.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck replies to Wallace M. Alexander's letter of December 20, thanking him for holiday greetings and wedding congratulations. Regarding the San Francisco immigration commissioner vacancy, Hornbeck notes Alexander's suggestions and queries whether he has contacted the Secretary of Labor. Regarding Jewish policy, Hornbeck relays the Japanese Foreign Office spokesman's public declaration that the German-Japanese cultural agreement has no connection with the treatment of Jewish residents and will not discriminate against German teachers in Japan, while noting in strict confidence that Berlin and Tokyo likely maintain an understanding restricting entry passports for German Jews.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Wallace M. Alexander Regarding Immigration Appointment and Treatment of Jews in Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference to a consular report from Kobe regarding Japanese restrictions on transit visas for European Jewish refugees.
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference sheet for a voluntary report dated May 22, 1941, from Consul Matthew J. Sokobin in Kobe, originally filed under 811.111 Refugees/1536. The report describes instructions given by the Japanese government to its consulates in Europe to halt the issuance of transit visas to Jewish refugees until the backlog of refugees in Japan had decreased. It notes that despite close political ties with Germany, there were no reported cases of discrimination against Jewish refugees in Japan, and local press comment was not unkind.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Voluntary Report from Kobe on Japanese Policy Toward Jewish Refugees
